# Setup Appendix: Docker and Git on Your Own Machine {#sec-setup .unnumbered}

@sec-containers teaches what a container is and why pinning a
base image by digest matters. This appendix is narrower and more
mundane. Its subject is getting Docker itself to run at all, on
the machines most readers actually sit down at, before any of
that chapter's content applies. We take up Docker on `arm64`
laptops, `--platform linux/amd64` emulation and its consequences,
Windows and WSL2, and locked-down institutional laptops. We add no
reproducibility theory here. The appendix is a checklist for the
moment before the first `docker build` succeeds. Its last two
sections do the same for git, which @sec-version-control needs
earlier in the course: a preflight to run once per machine
before the first commit ([Git preflight](setup-appendix.qmd#sec-git-preflight)), and a table of the
refusals a new user meets most often ([When git refuses](setup-appendix.qmd#sec-git-refuses)).

## Apple Silicon (M-series Mac)

@sec-containers already explains the mechanism. The Rocker images
differ. `rocker/r-ver`, the base of the showcase Dockerfile, is
published for both `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`, so on an Apple
Silicon Mac (an `arm64` host) it builds natively without any flag.
`rocker/tidyverse` and `rocker/verse` at 4.4.0, the bases of the
tidyverse and publishing profiles, publish a `linux/amd64` entry
only, so the Mac has nothing native to match, and the flag
`--platform linux/amd64` is not an optimization but the only way
to get a build at all. For either kind of base, the flag is what
makes a Mac build the same image that a CI runner or an `x86`
cluster builds, which is why this book passes it to every build.
That section of @sec-containers is worth reading before this
one. What follows is the practical sequence for a reader sitting
at such a machine for the first time.

1. **Confirm Docker Desktop is installed and running.** `docker
   version` should print both a `Client` and a `Server` block; a
   `Client`-only response, or a connection error, means the
   command is installed but Docker Desktop is not running.

2. **Add `--platform linux/amd64` to every build and run**:
   `docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t myimage .`. Against an
   `amd64`-only image such as `rocker/tidyverse:4.4.0`, omitting
   the flag does not silently succeed at native speed; it fails to
   resolve a matching entry at all. Against a multi-architecture
   image such as `rocker/r-ver`, omitting it does silently succeed,
   natively, and yields an `arm64` image that differs from the one
   the rest of the lab and the cluster run.

3. **Expect the build to be slower, not wrong.** Docker's own
   documentation on multi-platform builds warns that QEMU
   emulation 'can be much slower than native builds,
   especially for compute-heavy tasks' [@docker2024multiplatform].
   A `renv::restore()` that compiles several packages from source
   is exactly that kind of task; budget minutes, not seconds, for
   a first build, and do not read slowness alone as a broken
   Dockerfile.

4. **Confirm emulation is actually what is happening**, rather
   than guessing from slowness alone. `docker image inspect
   myimage --format '{{.Architecture}}'` reports the architecture
   of the image that was actually pulled or built; `amd64` on an
   Apple Silicon host confirms QEMU emulation is in play. The
   build log itself also names the platform at the top of each
   stage (`[linux/amd64 ...]`) when `--platform` was passed
   explicitly.

## Windows with WSL2

This book's images are Linux-based, and Docker Desktop on Windows
runs them through the **WSL2 backend**. It does not run them
through Hyper-V alone, nor through Windows containers, which
target Windows-native images this book never builds. Docker's own
current documentation describes the setup directly (opened
2026-10-12). WSL2 itself must be installed, and the Docker Desktop
setting **Use WSL 2 based engine** must be enabled under
Settings > General (on by default on systems that support it).
A specific
Linux distribution is then enabled for Docker integration under
Settings > Resources > WSL Integration, which is on by default for
the default distribution [@dockerdesktopwsl2024]. Installing WSL2 itself, if it is not
already present, is a single elevated command from Windows:
`wsl --install`, per Microsoft's own documentation
[@mswslinstall2024].

The problem that costs real time is where the project's files
live. Microsoft's own guidance is explicit: for the fastest
performance when working from a Linux command line, store files
in the WSL Linux filesystem (`/home/<user>/project`), not on a
mounted Windows drive accessed through `/mnt/c/...`. The same
document calls out such a mount as measurably slower
[@mswslfiles2024].
A repository cloned from inside Windows Explorer or PowerShell,
then opened from a WSL2 terminal only by crossing the `/mnt/c`
mount, pays this cost on every file Docker touches during a
build. The fix is to run `git clone` from inside the WSL2
terminal itself, so the repository lands under the Linux
filesystem from the start, not to move a Windows-cloned copy
afterward.

A second, quieter hazard travels with the same mount boundary:
line endings. Git on Windows commonly checks out text files with
CRLF line endings by default (`core.autocrlf=true`), while this
book's shell scripts, Dockerfiles, and R scripts assume LF, the
Linux convention a container's shell expects. A script that
looks identical in an editor can fail inside a container with
`/bin/bash^M: bad interpreter: No such file or directory` when a
shell runs it, or a bare `no such file or directory` when the
container runtime executes it directly. The reason is that a
trailing `\r` is part of the first line's interpreter path as far
as the kernel is concerned, and no interpreter of that name
exists. Cloning inside WSL2's own
filesystem, where Git's Linux default is LF, avoids this
entirely; cloning on the Windows side and later copying into WSL2
does not.

## Locked-down institutional laptops

A reader with no administrator rights cannot install Docker
Desktop at all, and nothing on the laptop itself will fix
this. The options instead route around it through other
infrastructure, in roughly increasing order of how much it is
worth asking for:

- **A cloud-hosted development environment.** @sec-backends
  already covers GitHub Codespaces, built on the Development
  Containers specification [@devcontainers]. There it is
  presented as a way to open a pinned environment in an editor
  without installing anything
  locally beyond a browser or a thin client. It requires no local
  Docker Desktop at all, because the container runs on GitHub's
  infrastructure, not the laptop.

- **A department-provided remote server or HPC login node,**
  reached over SSH. @sec-backends's HPC worked example already
  shows the companion half of this. Apptainer, not Docker, is the
  standard container runtime on a shared cluster, and it runs
  unprivileged. That is exactly the property that makes it
  acceptable where a locked-down laptop's Docker daemon is not.
  A reader who already has cluster access may find the
  institutional gap is already closed, just not with Docker.

- **A formal request to institutional IT**, when neither of the
  above is available. The request is answerable only if it is
  concrete. Ask specifically for Docker Desktop. If desktop
  software cannot be approved, ask instead for Docker Engine plus
  the ability to run containers under the requester's own
  account. Do not ask merely for 'Docker', which names a product
  family spanning both. An IT request phrased as 'I need Docker'
  is easy to deny or stall. On the other hand, one phrased as 'I
  need to run `docker build` and `docker run` as my own user,
  without root' is a specification someone can actually approve
  or substitute for.

## Diagnosing a failed or unexpectedly slow build

When a build fails or crawls, work through this sequence before
assuming the Dockerfile itself is wrong:

| Check | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `docker info` | Confirms Docker Desktop is actually running and reachable; also reports the server's architecture. |
| `docker version` | Separates client-only output (Desktop not running) from a full client-and-server response. |
| Is `--platform` set, and does the base image publish an `arm64` entry? | An `amd64`-only base on an `arm64` host needs the flag explicitly, and a missing flag there is a pull failure, not a slow build. A multi-architecture base such as `rocker/r-ver` builds without it, natively, but then yields an `arm64` image rather than the `amd64` one CI and the cluster run. |
| Docker Desktop's allotted disk and memory (Settings > Resources) | A build that stalls rather than errors often has hit a memory or disk ceiling Docker Desktop itself enforces, independent of the host machine's total resources. |
| On WSL2, is the project on the Windows filesystem (reached as `/mnt/c/...`) rather than in WSL2's own Linux filesystem (`/home/<user>/...`)? | A Windows-side clone is the likely source of a build that is slow specifically on Windows and not elsewhere; cloning again from inside the WSL2 terminal, into the Linux filesystem, is the fix. |

On the machine this book was written on (Apple Silicon, Docker
Desktop with the `desktop-linux` context), `docker version`
reports a `darwin/arm64` client against a `linux/arm64` server
(verified, run 2026-10-12). A reader passing
`--platform linux/amd64`, as this book does for every build,
would see the pulled or built image itself report `amd64` under
`docker image inspect`. The daemon underneath, however, is still
`arm64`. This combination is the signature of emulation working
as intended rather than a misconfiguration.

## Git preflight {#sec-git-preflight}

@sec-version-control assumes four things about git: it is
installed, it knows who the analyst is, it names a new
repository's first branch `main`, and the forge accepts the
analyst's credentials. On a fresh installation none of the
four can be taken for granted. The checks below are run once
per machine, before the first commit. Each names the chapter of
*Happy Git and GitHub for the useR* [@bryanhappygit] that treats
the step at length, with the RStudio detail this book omits.

1. **Git is installed.** `git --version` prints one line, such
   as `git version 2.56.0` on the machine this book was written
   on. A 'command not found' error means git must be installed
   first; see 'Install Git'
   (<https://happygitwithr.com/install-git.html>).

2. **Git knows who you are.** Every commit records a name and an
   e-mail address, so set both once:

   ```bash
   git config --global user.name 'A. Analyst'
   git config --global user.email 'analyst@example.org'
   ```

   Without them, git does one of two things. Where it cannot
   guess an address, it refuses the commit with 'Author identity
   unknown' and '\*\*\* Please tell me who you are.' Where it can,
   it builds an address from the login name and the host name,
   commits under it, and prints only a notice that the identity
   was 'configured automatically'. The second outcome is the
   worse one, because the commit succeeds under an address no
   collaborator would recognize. Use the address registered with
   the forge account. See 'Introduce yourself to Git'
   (<https://happygitwithr.com/hello-git.html>).

3. **New repositories start on `main`.** Unless told otherwise,
   git 2.56.0 names the first branch `master`, with a hint that
   the default will change in Git 3.0. The chapter's
   `git init -b main` handles this per repository; one setting
   handles it for all of them:

   ```bash
   git config --global init.defaultBranch main
   ```

   Afterward, `git config --global --list` should show three
   lines, `user.name`, `user.email`, and `init.defaultbranch`
   (git prints the key in lowercase).

4. **The forge accepts your credentials.** For git operations
   over HTTPS, GitHub does not accept the website password. It
   needs a personal access token, which a credential helper
   keeps in the operating system's store; see 'Personal access
   token for HTTPS' (<https://happygitwithr.com/https-pat.html>).
   Alternatively, `gh auth login` (the GitHub command-line
   client) signs in through a browser and stores a token, and
   `gh auth setup-git` makes git use it. The other route is an
   SSH key registered with the forge; see 'Set up keys for SSH'
   (<https://happygitwithr.com/ssh-keys.html>). A token never
   goes in `.Renviron` or anywhere else inside the repository.

5. **Line endings, on Windows only.** Cloning inside WSL2
   avoids the CRLF hazard described above. A repository that
   is also cloned on the Windows side should commit a
   `.gitattributes` file with the line `*.sh text eol=lf`, and
   the same for any other file a container executes; the
   attribute fixes LF on checkout whatever each user's
   `core.autocrlf` is. Failing that, set
   `git config --global core.autocrlf input`, under which git
   performs no conversion on checkout.

6. **A first push.** Create the repository on the forge
   *empty*, with no README, license, or `.gitignore`. Each of
   those makes a first commit that the local repository does
   not share. The push is then refused, and so is the pull
   meant to repair it (the 'fetch first' and 'unrelated
   histories' rows of @tbl-git-refuses). Then, in the local
   repository:

   ```bash
   git remote add origin https://github.com/lab/diabetes-cohort.git
   git push -u origin main
   ```

   Success ends with the line
   `branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.` See 'Connect
   to GitHub'
   (<https://happygitwithr.com/push-pull-github.html>) and
   'Existing project, GitHub last'
   (<https://happygitwithr.com/existing-github-last.html>).

## When git refuses {#sec-git-refuses}

The messages in @tbl-git-refuses are quoted as git 2.56.0 printed
them, on macOS, in scratch repositories built for this appendix
on 2026-11-08, shortened where an ellipsis appears. Two rows are
the exception and say so: their messages come from the forge,
not from git, and were not reproduced. The table follows the
model of the Docker table above: find the symptom, then read
across.

| Symptom (what git prints) | Cause | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| `Author identity unknown` ... `*** Please tell me who you are.` | No `user.name` or `user.email` is set, and git cannot guess one. | Set both ([Git preflight](setup-appendix.qmd#sec-git-preflight), step 2) and repeat the commit. If git guessed instead, fix the last commit with `git commit --amend --reset-author`, which git itself suggests. |
| A refused HTTPS push reporting that password authentication was removed (the forge's message, quoted in the Happy Git chapter on tokens; not reproduced) | The account password was given where the forge requires a token. | Store a personal access token through a credential helper or `gh auth login`, or switch the remote to SSH (step 4). |
| `! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first)` and `Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not have locally.` | The remote branch holds commits the local one lacks, because a collaborator pushed first or the forge made a first commit, and git will not overwrite them. | `git pull`, then `git push`. If the pull stops with `fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches.`, run `git pull --no-rebase` to merge (or set `pull.rebase false` once). Never force-push a shared branch. |
| `fatal: refusing to merge unrelated histories` | The local and forge repositories were started separately, typically with a README made on the forge. | If the forge's commit holds only template files, `git pull --no-rebase --allow-unrelated-histories origin main` joins the two once. Next time, create the forge repository empty or start by cloning it. |
| `You are in 'detached HEAD' state.`; `git status` reports `HEAD detached at` and a hash | A commit or tag was checked out rather than a branch. | Look around freely; `git switch main` returns. To keep commits made there, `git switch -c <new-branch-name>` first, as git's own advice says. |
| `CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in analysis.R` and `Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.` | Both branches changed the same lines. | Edit the file down to one version and delete the markers, then `git add` and `git commit`; or `git merge --abort` (@sec-version-control). |
| `error: src refspec main does not match any` | There is no local branch named `main`: either nothing has been committed yet, or the branch is `master`. | Make the first commit; check the name with `git branch --show-current`; rename with `git branch -m main`; push again. |
| A push refused for a file that exceeds the forge's size limit, 100 MiB on GitHub [@githublargefiles] (the forge's message; not reproduced) | A data file or a large output was committed. | First ask whether it holds PHI; if so, the exposure procedure of @sec-version-control comes before any git command. If the file is only in the last unpushed commit, `git rm --cached <file>`, ignore it, and `git commit --amend` (or `git reset HEAD~1` if it was the commit's only file). If it is deeper in the history, rewrite with `git filter-repo`. |

: Git refusals a new user meets, indexed by the message git or the forge prints. Messages from git 2.56.0, run 2026-11-08; the two forge rows were not reproduced. {#tbl-git-refuses}
